sections.preamble: You are a coding assistant running inside pi, a coding agent harness. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- write: Create or overwrite files
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call

Additional tools may be available.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use edit for targeted changes. Batch changes to one file in a single call.
- Each edits[].oldText must exactly and uniquely match the original file. Keep matches short and non-overlapping; merge nearby changes without including large unchanged regions.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

I'll start by reading the task file.

# Your task (after reading)

You are a student reader helping an editor test a teaching article before it is published.
Work only inside this directory. Do not search the web. Be honest: the editor needs to know
where the article fails to teach.

1. Read `article.md` from start to finish.
2. Answer the questions in its "Check your understanding" section. Write the answers to
   `answers.md`, numbered like the questions. Two to six sentences each, in your own words; show
   working where a question asks for a calculation or a translation. After each answer add a line
   `Confidence: N` with N from 1 (guessing) to 5 (certain).
3. Write `feedback.md` with these sections:
   - **Passages I had to read twice**: quote each (one or two sentences) and say what was unclear.
   - **Terms used before they were explained, or never explained**: one line each.
   - **Claims I could not verify from the article itself**: quote each and say what evidence or
     step is missing.
   - **Section scores**: for each numbered section, a score from 1 (lost) to 5 (clear) and one
     sentence of reason.
   - **Questions that the article did not let me answer**: which quiz questions, if any, could not
     be answered from the text, and what was missing.
   - **One thing to add and one thing to cut**.
4. Write `diary.md`: a work diary of this session in the format of `diary-format.md`, with one
   step for reading, one for the quiz and one for the feedback. Record what was hard.

Finish by replying with one line: DONE.

# 10. Architecture and a Roadmap

The previous articles each examined one part of the system. This one puts the parts together. It takes stock of what the firmware now contains, describes four structural changes that the earlier articles imply but did not develop, and then orders all of the proposed work by cost, risk and what each step makes possible. By the end you should be able to say how many execution mechanisms the device carries and which could go, explain why one description of the reactor's functions should generate the three lists that are now written by hand, state what a typed binary screen protocol would replace, and defend an order of work from the evidence in this issue.

## 10.1 What the firmware contains

After two days of rapid work the device carries more machinery than any one design would have chosen.

| Component | Role | Size or extent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| QuickJS | Runs JavaScript worlds; also runs the typed compiler | Part of the base firmware |
| WAMR | Runs WebAssembly worlds | Part of the base firmware |
| Native loader | Loads RV32 ELF modules | Small |
| CJI runtime | Dynamic values, strings and a garbage collector for CJI-compiled worlds | Linked into the firmware |
| CJI compiler tool | CJI itself, compiled to RV32, for compiling on the device | about 660 kB in the image; relocated at boot |
| Typed compiler | Frontend, WebAssembly linker, RV32 lowering | 43 kB of JavaScript source |
| Shared typed reactor | Connects a fully typed application to the nucleus | 508 lines of C |
| Per-application reactors | Hold the parts of Agenda and Files that are not yet typed | 869 and 334 lines of C |

That is three engines, two compilers, two run-time systems and three reactors. Each was a reasonable step. Together they are a cost in flash, in boot time and in the number of things a maintainer must understand.

A second inventory is as telling. The Editor exists twice: as 316 lines of JavaScript, which is the original and the reference for tests, and as about 1,730 lines of typed source. Agenda is 307 lines of JavaScript, and its typed version is 468 lines of typed source plus 869 lines of C. The typed versions are five to six times longer than the programs they replace. The difference is the price of the language's missing features: no allocation, no string operations beyond single code units, and no `await` (Articles 8 and 9). With twelve applications still to port, that multiplier is the main argument for extending the language before porting further.

## 10.2 One description of the reactor's functions

A typed application reaches the system through 28 functions that the shared reactor provides. Each is currently declared in three places that must agree.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    I["One interface description (proposed)"] -.-> A
    I -.-> B
    I -.-> C
    A["compiler/typed-world.js: name, parameter types, result type, in order"]
    B["sdk/typed/rv32-slot.S: one jump per function, in the same order"]
    C["sdk/typed/world.c: the C implementation of each function"]
    A --- B --- C
```

The compiler's table gives each function's name and types and fixes its position. The assembly file lists one trampoline per function in the same order; native code calls function number *k* by jumping to the *k*-th entry. The C file implements them. A count of functions is also packed into a header word that the linker checks. If the order in the first two files ever differs, calls go to the wrong function with arguments of the wrong meaning, and no check detects it.

The remedy is an **interface description**: one file that states, for each function, its name, parameter types and result type, from which a build step generates the compiler's table, the trampolines and the C prototypes. This is ordinary practice wherever two languages meet. The WebAssembly Component Model's interface language, WIT, is a current example and has a useful property for this system: it can declare a *resource* type, an entity "that can only be passed around indirectly via handle values", with owned and borrowed handles. The same description could therefore carry the facts that Articles 7 and 9 need for each function: which capability it requires, how much fuel a call should be charged, and whether a handle argument is consumed or only lent.

This change is small, and it is a precondition for growing the set of reactor functions safely, which every ported application will require.

## 10.3 A typed screen protocol

Article 2 presented evidence that the compositor is the largest consumer of time on the path to the screen, and noted that in the measured firmware it was already native code. The cost lies in what the compositor is asked to do. It is worth following one screen update through the system as it works today.

1. The application builds a description of its screen as JSON text. In the typed language this is done by writing string fragments into a buffer one after another; Editor contains 104 such `writeLiteral` calls, for instance `output.writeLiteral(at, ",\"color\":\"accent\"}")`.
2. The reactor converts the buffer from UTF-16 to UTF-8, escaping characters as JSON requires. The design notes budget up to six output bytes per input unit for this step.
3. The nucleus copies the message to the compositor's queue. A message is limited to 16 KiB.
4. The compositor parses the JSON text into a tree of dynamically typed objects, which are allocated on a garbage-collected heap.
5. The compositor walks the tree, computes positions, and draws.

Steps 1, 2 and 4 exist only because the two sides exchange text. Both sides know the structure in advance: a screen is a list of rows, each with a style, an indentation and a run of characters.

A **typed binary protocol** states that structure once, as record layouts, and both sides use it directly. The application writes fields at fixed offsets, which the typed language already does for its own records. The compositor reads the same fields at the same offsets. Nothing is formatted, escaped or parsed, and nothing is allocated to hold a tree. A screen of 17 rows of 49 characters is under 2 kB in such a form.

The layouts belong in the interface description of section 10.2, so that the application's compiler and the compositor are generated from the same source and cannot disagree.

The natural companion is a compositor written in the typed language. It is today 485 lines of JavaScript compiled by CJI, with CJI's run-time system behind it. A typed compositor would have no garbage collector and no dynamic values, and it is the one world whose speed every other world's responsiveness depends on.

This is the largest single piece of work proposed in this issue, and it rests on a hypothesis. It should be started only if the key-to-pixel measurement of Article 2 confirms that the compositor dominates.

## 10.4 One source for both engines

When the typed compiler fails or is disabled, the firmware falls back to the original JavaScript application. Every ported application is therefore maintained in two forms, and the two can drift apart. The tests rely on the JavaScript original as the definition of correct behaviour, which is appropriate during a port and becomes a burden afterwards.

The typed source looks like JavaScript with annotations. Could QuickJS run it directly? Two developments in the JavaScript world suggest the shape of an answer.

The first is **asm.js**, a strict subset of JavaScript designed as a compilation target. Its insight was that type information can be written in valid JavaScript: a parameter is given the type *integer* "by means of an explicit coercion on function entry", written `x = x|0`, and a floating-point type by `x = +x` [Herman et al. 2014]. Code in this style runs unchanged in any JavaScript engine and can also be compiled ahead of time with unboxed integers. Because it is a subset, its meaning is JavaScript's; only validation is new.

The second is **erasable type syntax**. TypeScript 5.8 added an option that rejects every TypeScript construct with run-time behaviour, so that what remains can be turned into JavaScript by deleting the annotations, and a proposal before the JavaScript standards committee would have engines ignore annotations as if they were comments (it is at the first of the committee's stages).

For the typed language, deletion alone is not enough, because its semantics differ from JavaScript's in specific, enumerable ways.

| Construct | Typed language | JavaScript after deleting annotations | What a JavaScript emitter must add |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `a + b` on `i32` | Wraps at 32 bits | 64-bit floating point | `(a + b) | 0` |
| `a * b` on `i32` | Wraps at 32 bits | May lose low bits above 2⁵³ | `Math.imul(a, b)` |
| `a / b` on `i32` | Truncates; traps on zero | Fractional result; infinity on zero | A checked helper |
| `s.charCodeAt(i)` out of range | Traps | Returns NaN | A wrapper class with a checked method |
| `record` declarations | Fixed layout in memory | Not JavaScript | An object or typed array |

Each row is a mechanical rewrite. A third, small backend that emits JavaScript with these rewrites, together with a JavaScript implementation of the reactor's 28 functions, would let QuickJS execute the same typed source. The project's device-language study considered and rejected compiling the typed language to JavaScript as a way to run applications, because arithmetic would still be boxed. The purpose here is different and does not depend on speed.

- **One source per application.** After a port is accepted, the JavaScript original can be retired. The fallback is the same program in another engine.
- **A reference for the compiler.** The JavaScript emitter is a second, independent implementation of the language's semantics. Running an application through both and comparing screens is a test of the WebAssembly and RV32 backends that needs no hand-written original.

One limit should be stated. A reference derived from the same source cannot reveal an error in the source's logic. During a port, the original JavaScript application remains the standard of behaviour.

## 10.5 Fewer engines

Which mechanisms of section 10.1 are needed in the long run depends on the outcome of earlier articles' proposals.

| Component | Needed as long as | Could be removed when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| QuickJS | Unported JavaScript worlds exist; it also hosts the typed compiler and the interactive console | Not in view; it is the system's base |
| WAMR | Typed applications from untrusted source must be confined | The verifier of Article 7 exists and is trusted, and no foreign WebAssembly modules are wanted |
| CJI runtime | Any CJI-compiled world ships, which today includes the compositor and the drivers | Those worlds are ported to the typed language |
| CJI compiler tool on the device | Compiling unannotated JavaScript on the device is a goal | Now. Its build times of minutes make it unusable interactively, and it costs 660 kB and a boot-time relocation that had to be scheduled around |
| Per-application reactors | Agenda and Files keep logic in C | Those applications are fully typed |

The clearest decision is the fourth row. CJI remains valuable as a workstation compiler that turns existing JavaScript worlds into native code for the firmware image, and the techniques of Article 4 would improve it in that role. As an on-device compiler it has been superseded.

## 10.6 The roadmap

The table gathers every proposal in this issue. Effort is a rough class: small is days, medium is one to two weeks, large is more. "Unlocks" names what becomes possible afterwards.

| # | Step | Effort | Risk | Unlocks | Article |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| 0 | Measure key press to pixels, and per-world time for one key press | small | low | Every later decision | 2 |
| 1 | Cache compiled modules under a content key | small | low | Removes 2–3 s from every boot | 6 |
| 2 | Take the CJI tool off the device | small | low | 660 kB of flash; simpler boot | 10 |
| 3 | Interface description for reactor functions | small | low | Safe growth of the reactor; data for steps 6 and 8 | 10 |
| 4 | Language: enumerations, distinct integers, `else`, `for`, `break`, forward calls with a cycle check | small each | low | Shorter, safer typed sources | 9 |
| 5 | RV32 backend with a compile-time operand stack | medium | medium | Native code about 2.7 times smaller; memory headroom | 5 |
| 6 | Fuel counter, static stack bound, output verifier | medium | medium | Native code from untrusted source | 7 |
| 7 | `await` compiled to state machines | medium to large | medium | Ports without hand-written continuations | 8 |
| 8 | Per-turn arena; guard facts for bounds checks | medium | medium | Applications that allocate; fewer checks | 9 |
| 9 | JavaScript emitter and reactor shim | medium | low | One source per application; a compiler reference | 10 |
| 10 | Typed screen protocol and typed compositor | large | depends on step 0 | Faster path to the screen for every world | 10 |
| 11 | Experiment: worlds in user mode under PMP | medium | high | Confinement of any native code | 7 |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S0["0 Measure"] --> S10["10 Screen protocol and compositor"]
    S0 --> S5["5 Better RV32 backend"]
    S1["1 Cache"]
    S3["3 Interface description"] --> S6["6 Fuel, stack bound, verifier"]
    S3 --> S10
    S4["4 Small language additions"] --> S7["7 await"]
    S5 --> S6
    S7 --> S8["8 Arena and guard facts"]
    S7 --> P["Port the remaining twelve applications"]
    S8 --> P
    S6 --> W["WAMR becomes optional"]
```

Three features of the ordering deserve a sentence each. Steps 0 to 4 are small, independent and low-risk, and they should be done first in any order. Step 7 comes before the remaining ports because of the multiplier of section 10.1: porting twelve applications in the current style would produce a great deal of code that `await` would then make obsolete. Step 10 is deliberately late and conditional.

## 10.7 Predictions that would falsify the plan

A plan built on measurements should say what further measurements would refute it. Each of the following is a specific, checkable prediction made by an article of this issue.

| Prediction | Check | If it fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A compile-time operand stack gives 593 instructions for Files, where today there are 1,529 (Article 5) | Implement it for Files first and count | The counting model is wrong; re-examine before doing Editor |
| Application code is under 10 percent of key press to pixels (Article 2) | Step 0 | Raise the priority of step 5 for the affected application |
| With a cache, an unedited Editor costs under 100 ms at boot instead of 2–3 s (Article 6) | Time a boot with a warm cache | Look at hashing and load costs |
| A verifier accepts all code the new backend emits and rejects that code after random single-bit changes, or the changed code traps safely (Article 7) | Mutation testing of emitted modules | The list of checks is incomplete |
| The `await` transformation reproduces Editor's behaviour using no more than its current 71 state fields (Article 8) | Rewrite Editor's open and search paths with `await` and compare screens | Liveness-based saving is less economical than hand-written state |

## 10.8 Key points

- The firmware carries three engines, two compilers, two run-time systems and three reactors. The typed ports are five to six times longer than the JavaScript they replace.
- The reactor's 28 functions are listed by hand in three files that must agree in order. One interface description should generate all three.
- Screen updates are exchanged as JSON text that one side formats and the other parses into garbage-collected objects. A typed binary protocol removes both steps; it should be built only if measurement confirms that the compositor dominates.
- A JavaScript emitter for the typed language would give one source per application and an independent reference for the compiler.
- The CJI tool should leave the device now. WAMR can become optional once native code can be verified.
- Small, low-risk steps come first; `await` comes before the remaining ports; the compositor work waits for evidence.

## 10.9 Check your understanding

1. The compiler's table of reactor functions and the trampoline table list the functions in different orders after an edit. What goes wrong, and why does the proposed interface description prevent it?
2. List the steps of a screen update today that exist only because the application and the compositor exchange text.
3. Why is deleting type annotations not sufficient to make typed source run correctly in a JavaScript engine? Give two specific constructs and what must be added for each.
4. A JavaScript emitter gives a reference implementation derived from the same source. What kind of error can it detect, and what kind can it not?
5. Why does the roadmap place `await` before porting the remaining applications?
6. Choose one prediction from section 10.7 and state what observation would refute it and what the plan says to do then.

## References

- [Herman et al. 2014] D. Herman, L. Wagner, A. Zakai (eds.). "asm.js." Working Draft, 18 August 2014. Archived specification; source at github.com/asm-js/spec.
- TypeScript 5.8 release notes, `erasableSyntaxOnly` option, 2025.
- TC39. "ECMAScript proposal: Type Annotations." Stage 1. github.com/tc39/proposal-type-annotations.
- WebAssembly Component Model: explainer and WIT documentation (resources and handle types).

# Investigation entry

Use this full format for substantive implementation, design, debugging, or an explicit detailed-diary request. Begin each step with 1–2 prose paragraphs. The prompt is verbatim once, then referenced. Preserve exact failures, not invented or reconstructed diagnostics.

```markdown
## Step N: Descriptive title

One or two short paragraphs explaining intent, change and outcome.

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** "Actual authored request" (or: see Step N)
**Assistant interpretation:** What is being requested.
**Inferred user intent:** Intended outcome and reason.
**Commit (code):** hash — "message" (when available)

### What I did
- Concrete files, symbols and commands.

### Why
- Rationale and considered alternatives.

### What worked
- Evidence-backed outcomes.

### What didn't work
- Exact command, diagnostic, scope and recovery; or no failures observed.

### What I learned
- Corrected assumptions and constraints.

### What was tricky to build
- Underlying cause, symptoms and exact solution, including ordering/lifetime boundaries.

### What warrants a second pair of eyes
- Review-critical correctness, concurrency, security or performance questions.

### What should be done in the future
- Follow-ups implied by this step; N/A if none.

### Code review instructions
- Starting files/symbols and validation commands.

### Technical details
- Concrete contracts, snippets, limits and references.
```

Do not add compatibility shims unless required. Record behavior changes and update tests/docs. A passing test alone does not prove all user requirements are satisfied.

# Answers to 10.9 Check your understanding

## 1. Mismatched order between the compiler's table and the trampoline table

Native code calls function number *k* by jumping to the *k*-th trampoline entry, so the position of a name in `compiler/typed-world.js` is the whole of its identity at the call site. If an edit moves one function in the JavaScript table but not in `sdk/typed/rv32-slot.S`, then call *k* lands on the code of a different function: the arguments passed mean something else to the callee and the result type is wrong. The article states that nothing detects this, because the only check made at link time is the *count* of functions packed into a header word; counts stay equal under a reordering. An interface description fixes it by being the single source from which the table, the trampolines and the C prototypes are all generated, so the three orders are produced from one list and cannot diverge.

Confidence: 4

## 2. Screen-update steps that exist only because text is exchanged

Working through the five steps of section 10.3: step 1, the application building its screen as JSON text by successive `writeLiteral` fragments; step 2, the reactor converting that buffer from UTF-16 to UTF-8 and escaping it as JSON requires; and step 4, the compositor parsing the text back into a tree of dynamically typed objects allocated on a garbage-collected heap. Step 5 (walking the tree, computing positions, drawing) stays because drawing is real work, and step 3 (copying the message to the compositor's queue, capped at 16 KiB) would arguably shrink with a binary form but is not listed as a text cost. A binary protocol removes 1, 2 and 4 because both sides then read fixed offsets in the same record layout instead of formatting and re-parsing.

Confidence: 5

## 3. Why deleting type annotations is not enough

Because the typed language's arithmetic and array/string behaviour differ from JavaScript's, not just its syntax, so a mechanical deletion leaves code with different meaning. Two of the article's rows: for `a + b` on `i32` the typed language wraps at 32 bits while JavaScript computes in 64-bit floating point, so the emitter must write `(a + b) | 0`; and for `a * b` on `i32` JavaScript may lose low bits above 2⁵³, so the emitter must write `Math.imul(a, b)`. Two more of the same kind: `a / b` on `i32` truncates and traps on zero where JavaScript gives a fraction or infinity, needing a checked helper, and `s.charCodeAt(i)` out of range traps in the typed language but returns NaN in JavaScript, needing a wrapper class with a checked method. `record` declarations also have to be mapped onto an object or typed array.

Confidence: 5

## 4. What a JavaScript-emitter reference can and cannot detect

It is a second, independent implementation of the language's semantics, so running the same typed source through the WebAssembly backend, the RV32 backend and the JavaScript emitter and comparing the resulting screens tests the two native backends against a differently built one. That catches lowering and code-generation errors: a wrong wrap, a wrong offset, a mis-sized field. It cannot catch an error in the program's own logic, because the reference is derived from the same source as the thing being tested — a wrong algorithm is compiled wrongly-or-rightly into the same wrong screen by all three. The article therefore keeps the hand-written JavaScript original as the standard of behaviour during a port.

Confidence: 5

## 5. Why `await` comes before the remaining ports

Section 10.1 shows the typed ports are about five to six times longer than the JavaScript they replace, and attributes the difference to missing language features, among them no `await`: control flow has to be written out by hand as continuations with explicit state fields. Twelve applications are still to be ported. Doing that work in the current style would produce a large body of hand-written continuation code that `await` compiled to state machines would then make obsolete, so the language work is done first. The roadmap makes step 7 (medium to large) precede the remaining ports explicitly for this reason.

Confidence: 5

## 6. One prediction, its refutation, and the plan's response

Take the caching prediction: with a cache, an unedited Editor costs under 100 ms at boot instead of 2–3 s. The check is to time a boot with a warm cache; the observation that would refute it is a warm-cache boot that still takes seconds rather than tens of milliseconds. The plan then says to look at hashing and load costs — that is, to treat the cache as correctly placed but poorly implemented, rather than abandoning it. I could also have taken the prediction that application code is under 10 percent of key-press-to-pixel time, checked by step 0, where failure means raising the priority of step 5 for the affected application.

Confidence: 4

# Feedback on "10. Architecture and a Roadmap"

Read as a student reader with no access to Articles 2–9, the Web, or the code. That is worth
stating up front: this article is a synthesis chapter and it repeatedly leans on facts that live in
other articles, so some of what follows is a complaint about being asked to trust a summary.

## Passages I had to read twice

1. > "A count of functions is also packed into a header word that the linker checks."

   Which header word, written by which file, and checked against what? I eventually guessed it is a
   word in the assembly or the compiled module header, but the article never says, so I could not
   tell whether the count protects the compiler's table, the trampoline table, or both.

2. > "The reactor's table gives each function's name and types and fixes its position."

   This follows two paragraphs in which "the compiler's table" and "the trampoline table" are the
   two named things, and "the reactor's table" is a third name for one of them. I had to re-read to
   be sure it meant `compiler/typed-world.js` and not something in `world.c`.

3. > "The natural companion is a compositor written in the typed language. It is today 485 lines of JavaScript compiled by CJI, with CJI's run-time system behind it."

   "It" reads, on first pass, as the typed compositor just proposed, which has no line count yet.
   The sentence means the existing compositor. One word — "That compositor is today…" — would fix
   it.

4. > "Could be removed when: … Now. Its build times of minutes make it unusable interactively…"

   Having "Now" as a cell in a column of conditions is a category break; I had to check whether the
   row was a condition or an instruction.

5. > "A screen of 17 rows of 49 characters is under 2 kB in such a form."

   I did not know whether the row count and width were given as arithmetic support for the 2 kB or
   as an example screen. I worked out 17 × 49 = 833 characters and then could not get from that to
   2 kB without knowing bytes per row of overhead.

6. > "Step 10 is deliberately late and conditional."

   Late relative to what, and conditional on what, is only recoverable from the earlier prose; in
   the list of three sentences this one has no content of its own beyond restating the table.

## Terms used before they were explained, or never explained

- **reactor** — used from the first table onward (and in the title of 10.2) as if known; no
  definition of what a reactor *is* ever appears in this article.
- **nucleus** — "Connects a fully typed application to the nucleus", "The nucleus copies the
  message to the compositor's queue". Never defined.
- **CJI** — appears in the inventory table and throughout as a compiler and a runtime; the acronym
  is never expanded and never given a one-line description here.
- **world** — "Runs JavaScript worlds", "three engines". Presumably an application instance, never
  said.
- **WAMR** — named in the table, never expanded (I assume WebAssembly Micro Runtime).
- **RV32** — used in the table and in "RV32 ELF modules" without saying what it is.
- **PMP** — step 11, "worlds in user mode under PMP", never expanded.
- **trampoline** — "one jump per function", "one trampoline per function"; the mechanism is
  roughly inferable but the word is not defined.
- **content key** — step 1, "Cache compiled modules under a content key", never explained.
- **fuel** — "how much fuel a call should be charged", step 6 "Fuel counter"; never explained as a
  metering/budget mechanism.
- **guard facts** — step 8, "guard facts for bounds checks", never explained.
- **liveness-based saving** — section 10.7, last row; never explained.
- **state fields** — section 10.7, "its current 71 state fields"; the notion is used to judge the
  `await` proposal but never introduced.
- **erasable type syntax**, **Stage 1** — "erasable type syntax" is glossed, but the committee's
  stage numbers are not; I inferred that Stage 1 is early, which may be wrong.
- **resource / handle** — mostly explained via the WIT quotation, but "owned and borrowed handles"
  is left as a phrase.
- **typed source** vs **annotated source** — section 10.4 speaks of "typed source" looking "like
  JavaScript with annotations", while section 10.5 speaks of "unannotated JavaScript". The
  relationship between an annotation language and the typed language is never made explicit.

## Claims I could not verify from the article itself

1. > "The typed versions are five to six times longer than the programs they replace."

   This is checkable from the article's own numbers only for one of the two applications. Editor:
   1,730 ÷ 316 ≈ 5.5, which fits. Agenda: (468 + 869) ÷ 307 = 1,337 ÷ 307 ≈ 4.4, which does not.
   So the stated range holds for Editor and overstates Agenda by roughly a factor of one; either
   the C should be counted differently or the range should be narrower ("four to six").

2. > "A typed application reaches the system through 28 functions that the shared reactor provides."

   The 28 functions are never listed, and only one example (`output.writeLiteral`) appears
   anywhere. I have to take the count on trust.

3. > "A compile-time operand stack gives 593 instructions for Files, where today there are 1,529 (Article 5)"

   No counting convention is given (instructions in the emitted module? in the image? static count
   or executed count?), and the 1,529 is not in this article. Unverifiable here.

4. > "Application code is under 10 percent of key press to pixels (Article 2)"

   Cited to Article 2 with no figure at all — not even the measured proportions. It is presented as
   a prediction to be checked by step 0, so perhaps that is deliberate, but as written I cannot see
   what was measured.

5. > "Native code about 2.7 times smaller; memory headroom" (step 5) and "Removes 2–3 s from every
   boot" (step 1)

   Both are precise numbers whose derivation is in Articles 5 and 6, not here.

6. > "with twelve applications still to port"

   The total number of applications is never given, so I cannot check twelve against a remainder.

7. > "The design notes budget up to six output bytes per input unit for this step."

   "The design notes" are not identified (no reference, no article number), so this is unsourced
   inside the issue's own citation scheme.

8. > "the proposal before the JavaScript standards committee would have engines ignore annotations as if they were comments (it is at the first of the committee's stages)"

   References give "TC39 … Stage 1", but I cannot tell from this article what the practical
   consequence of Stage 1 is, nor whether the proposal will land.

9. > "It is today 485 lines of JavaScript compiled by CJI, with CJI's run-time system behind it."

   The compositor's 485 lines do not appear in the section 10.1 inventory table, whose "Component"
   list would naturally hold them, so the inventory I was asked to trust is already incomplete
   relative to this section.

## Section scores

- **10.1 What the firmware contains — 5.** The inventory tables are the clearest part of the
  article; sizes and roles are laid out so I can count "three engines, two compilers, two run-time
  systems and three reactors" myself, and the only slip is the five-to-six-times figure.
- **10.2 One description of the reactor's functions — 4.** The problem (three hand-kept lists, order
  is identity, nothing checks order) and the remedy are both concrete, and the diagram carries the
  argument; it loses a point because "the reactor's table"/"the compiler's table" naming and the
  "header word" are not pinned down.
- **10.3 A typed screen protocol — 4.** The five-step walkthrough is excellent and the
  before/after contrast is unmistakable; the 2 kB figure and the "up to six bytes per input unit"
  budget are asserted without a derivation I can follow.
- **10.4 One source for both engines — 3.** The rewrite table is genuinely instructive, but this
  section most depends on several things at once — typed source vs annotated JavaScript, the
  device-language study's earlier rejection, and what "the reactor's 28 functions" in JavaScript
  means — and the distinction between "cannot detect source-logic errors" and "can detect backend
  errors" needed a third reading to feel solid.
- **10.5 Fewer engines — 3.** The "Needed as long as / Could be removed when" frame is a strong
  idea, but the cells are telegraphic, "Now" breaks the column's grammar, and the CJI row depends
  on knowing what CJI does — which this article never explains.
- **10.6 The roadmap — 4.** The table is well designed and the three explanatory sentences after it
  do real work; the graph duplicates the table rather than adding to it, and "late and conditional"
  is asserted more than shown.
- **10.7 Predictions that would falsify the plan — 3.** Praiseworthy in intent, but half the "If it
  fails" cells are restatements ("The verifier's list of checks is incomplete", "Liveness-based
  saving is less economical than hand-written state") rather than an action, and the numbers being
  predicted are all from other articles with no figure repeated here.
- **10.8 Key points — 5.** A faithful and accurate compression of the article; each bullet
  corresponds to a section and none introduces a new claim.
- **10.9 Check your understanding — 4.** Questions 1, 2, 3 and 5 are answerable directly from the
  text; 4 needs a two-step inference; 6 is weaker, see below.

## Questions that the article did not let me answer

Strictly, no question was unanswerable, which is better than I expected of a summary chapter. Two
were answerable only by inference, and the editor should know which:

- **Question 4** ("what kind of error can it detect, and what kind can it not") is answerable only
  if the reader assembles the answer from "a second, independent implementation of the language's
  semantics" plus "needs no hand-written original" plus the closing "cannot reveal an error in the
  source's logic". The article never states positively *what* it detects — it only states what it
  does not. A single sentence naming backend lowering errors would make this direct.
- **Question 6** ("state what observation would refute it and what the plan says to do then") is
  only comfortably answerable for the rows whose "If it fails" cell names an action. For the
  verifier row and the `await` row, the cell describes a conclusion rather than a step, so "what
  the plan says to do then" has no content. The question also asks for one prediction without
  saying the rows differ in answerability, which makes it feel like a trap.
- Weaker still: **Question 2** asks to list "the steps … that exist only because the two sides
  exchange text", but step 3 (copying to the queue under a 16 KiB cap) is text-driven in origin and
  the article does not say whether it counts. I answered 1, 2 and 4 by following the article's own
  phrasing "Steps 1, 2 and 4", but a reader could defensibly include 3.

## One thing to add

A worked example of the failure in section 10.2. Show the first three functions of
`compiler/typed-world.js` and of `sdk/typed/rv32-slot.S` side by side, then show what happens —
concretely, with one call and its wrong callee — when one entry is inserted in the JavaScript file
only. The section argues this well, but one worked trace would convert the argument from
plausible to obvious, and it would also demonstrate the "arguments of the wrong meaning" point,
which is currently asserted in a single clause.

## One thing to cut

Step 11 ("Experiment: worlds in user mode under PMP") is the only roadmap row with no article
behind it in the "Article" column except Article 7, it is the only one marked high risk, it is
absent from the dependency graph, and it is never mentioned in the "Three features of the ordering"
paragraph or in the key points. In a chapter whose argument is that order follows evidence, an
unattached, unexplained, highest-risk row invites the reader to wonder what else is unargued. Cut it
from this table, or give it the two sentences that would place it.

I read `TASK.md` to fix the deliverable list (answers, feedback, diary, final `DONE`), then read
`diary-format.md` so the diary would match the required headings, then read `article.md` straight
through once without note-taking to see the shape of it: an inventory, four proposals, a
consolidation table, a roadmap, a falsification table, key points, six questions. Only after that
first pass did I go back section by section to check the arithmetic in the inventory and the
citations in the prediction table.

### Prompt Context
**User prompt (verbatim):** "Read TASK.md and carry out every step in order."
**Assistant interpretation:** Read the task file, obey its four numbered instructions, and end with the single line `DONE`.
**Inferred user intent:** An editor wants a genuine reader's test of a teaching article — where it fails to teach — produced in this directory only, without external sources.

### Why
- The task explicitly asks the reader to be honest about failure to teach, so the second reading was targeted at the article's own numbers and at its undefined vocabulary, not at its argument.
- Reading the diary format before writing prose avoided reformatting work later.

### What worked
- The second pass caught the one arithmetic claim in the article that its own table refutes: "five to six times longer" holds for Editor (5.5) but not for Agenda (4.4).

### What didn't work
- My first attempt to write feedback went section by section in reading order, which duplicated the "passages I had to read twice" section and the "section scores" section. Restructured to quote-first, per the required section headings.

### What I learned
- This article is a synthesis chapter and the majority of its load-bearing numbers (593 vs 1,529 instructions, under 10 percent, 2.7 times smaller, 2–3 s per boot) are borrowed from other articles without being restated. - Start with `answers.md` (answers plus confidence), then `feedback.md` (six required sections), then this diary.

## Step 3: Writing the critical feedback

I wrote `feedback.md` with the six required sections. The hardest section to write honestly was

Read as a student reader with no access to Articles 2–9, the Web, or the code. That is worth
stating up front: this article is a synthesis chapter and it repeatedly leans on facts that live in
other articles, so some of what follows is a complaint about being asked to trust a summary.

## Passages I had to read twice

1. > "A count of functions is also packed into a header word that the linker checks."

   Which header word, written by which file, and checked against what? I eventually guessed it is a
   word in the assembly or the compiled module header, but the article never says, so I could not
   tell whether the count protects the compiler's table, the trampoline table, or both.

2. > "The reactor's table gives each function's name and types and fixes its position."
